China-Aligned Hackers Hijack Sogou Input Method DNS Requests to Deploy DarkVigil Backdoor

By Kamali

Researchers at ESET say a China-aligned group called SlippyNunchucks hijacked internet lookups made by the Windows version of Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language typing tool, to install a spying backdoor called DarkVigil. Tencent fixed the weakness in version 16.10, and users are urged to update.

A China-aligned hacking group has turned a popular Chinese-language typing program into a delivery route for spyware, according to research published by the security firm ESET on November 4, 2026. The group, which ESET calls SlippyNunchucks, abused the way the Windows version of Sogou Input Method fetched part of its settings, and used it to install a backdoor known as DarkVigil. Sogou Input Method is a widely used input method editor developed by Tencent.

How the attack worked

ESET says a component of Sogou Input Method requested a "brand-promotion" configuration from a Sogou server over plain, unencrypted HTTP. Because that traffic was not protected, the attackers could use DNS hijacking, a technique that quietly redirects a program's lookup to a different server, to send those requests to infrastructure they controlled. That server returned a malicious configuration instead of the real one.

The altered configuration then led a legitimate Sogou component to download files that included a signed program and a booby-trapped library of the same name that it loaded. This method, known as DLL side-loading, makes the malicious code run under the cover of a trusted program. The end result was the DarkVigil implant running on the victim's computer.

What DarkVigil is

DarkVigil, also known as FDMTP, is a modular toolset written in .NET with more than 20 plugins. ESET has tracked the malware and its operator since early 2025. The activity was described as part of a surveillance campaign, which points to espionage rather than ordinary financial crime.

Timeline and victims

ESET says the Sogou activity began on July 1, 2026, and that victims were spread across six countries. The activity followed an earlier supply-chain compromise involving the software QuickFox. The researchers saw the group switch to Sogou three days after QuickFox released a clean version. Other applications mentioned as having been abused by the same actor include QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam and tawk.to.

The number and spread of victims first made the researchers suspect a software exploit, but the investigation traced the problem to the insecure connection instead.

The fix

Tencent addressed the issue in Sogou Input Method version 16.10, released on October 30, 2026. According to security summaries of the research, the update moves the affected requests from HTTP to HTTPS and adds certificate validation, which prevents a redirected server from impersonating the real one. Users should update to version 16.10 or later. Security teams are advised to watch for unexpected files named after Adobe software inside Sogou's components folder and for unusual network connections from the app. ESET's report contains the full technical indicators.

Not the first Sogou problem

This is not the first time Sogou Input Method has been used this way. In September 2026, Gen Digital reported that a separate, now-patched flaw in the software was exploited by another China-linked group to deliver a different backdoor.

What is still unknown

ESET has not established where the DNS hijacking took place. The researchers say possibilities include compromised routers with altered DNS settings, routers carrying a DNS-hijacking implant, or interception at the level of an internet provider. It is also unclear how many people were ultimately infected, who the specific targets were, and whether the group has other delivery routes ready.

Why it matters

The case shows how a harmless-looking background request, such as one for a small image or settings file, can become an attack path when it is not encrypted. Because the traffic looked like normal application behaviour, victims had little chance of noticing. Users and organisations with Sogou Input Method installed should update it, check their router and DNS settings, and treat any software that still uses plain HTTP for updates or configuration as a risk.
